definition: An integer type used to hold a character code, whose size is defined to be one byte.
wrongs: A floating-point type that stores a string of unlimited length.
A pointer type that always addresses a string.
A signed 32-bit integer on every implementation.
why: The language defines the size of char as 1, and that byte is the unit in which every other object's size is measured.
example: A variable declared as char can store the code for one letter such as the letter A.
scenario: A program needs an integer object whose size is exactly one byte so it can hold one character code. Which type guarantees that size?
scenarioWhy: char is the integer type whose size is defined to be one byte.

definition: The basic signed integer type for whole numbers, required to be at least 16 bits wide.
wrongs: A floating type with a fractional part and about 15 decimal digits.
An unsigned type that cannot represent a negative value.
A character type whose size is always exactly one byte.
why: int is the natural integer for arithmetic, and the standard requires it to cover at least the range of a 16-bit signed value.
example: A loop counter declared as int can hold a negative value such as minus 1.
scenario: Portable code needs a signed whole-number type that is at least 16 bits wide. Which basic type guarantees that?
scenarioWhy: int is the signed integer type with a minimum width of 16 bits.

definition: A single-precision floating type, commonly 32 bits wide, that stores an approximate real number.
wrongs: An integer type that stores only exact whole numbers.
A double-precision floating type that is commonly 64 bits wide.
A pointer to a floating constant.
why: float offers a fractional range in a smaller format than double, with roughly seven decimal digits of precision.
example: A gain stored in a float approximates one tenth and is not required to be that exact fraction.
scenario: A value is stored as a 32-bit IEEE floating number rather than a 64-bit one. Which C type is the usual match?
scenarioWhy: Single-precision floating point is the float type.

definition: A double-precision floating type, commonly 64 bits wide, that approximates real numbers more precisely than float.
wrongs: A single-precision floating type that is commonly 32 bits wide.
A 64-bit integer with no fractional part.
A type required to be 128 bits on every platform.
why: An unsuffixed floating constant has type double, and the usual math-library functions take double arguments.
example: A literal such as two and a half has type double, and assigning it to a float may narrow it.
scenario: An unsuffixed floating literal is passed to a math function that expects the wider real type. Which type does the literal have?
scenarioWhy: C gives unsuffixed floating constants the type double.

definition: An operator that yields how many bytes a type or an object occupies.
wrongs: A function that returns the number of elements in any array after it has been passed to a function.
A function that returns how many characters precede a null terminator.
An operator that counts the bits in a value only while the program is running.
why: Object size is counted in units of char, and this operator reports that count for its operand.
example: Where int occupies 4 bytes, applying the operator to an int object yields 4.
scenario: A heap request must cover ten ints. Which operator provides the byte size of one int?
scenarioWhy: sizeof reports the storage width of the type so the allocation size can be computed.

definition: An integer that represents only zero and positive values and wraps modulo a power of two.
wrongs: A signed integer that can represent negative values.
A floating value that can represent a fraction.
A pointer, which the language defines as a signed integer.
why: Unsigned arithmetic is defined to wrap modulo 2 to the width, unlike signed overflow, which is undefined.
example: An 8-bit unsigned value of 255 becomes 0 when 1 is added.
scenario: An 8-bit unsigned variable holding 255 becomes 0 after 1 is added. Which rule produced that result?
scenarioWhy: Unsigned arithmetic wraps modulo 2 to the n, so 255 plus 1 is 0 in eight bits.

definition: The widening of a small integer to int, or to unsigned int, before an arithmetic operator is applied.
wrongs: The conversion of every integer to double before any arithmetic.
The truncation of every sum back to char after the operation.
The conversion of a pointer to a wider pointer type.
why: Arithmetic operators do not calculate in char or short width; the operands are widened first.
example: Adding the unsigned char values 200 and 100 can produce 300 because each value is widened before the addition.
scenario: Two unsigned char values, 200 and 100, are added and the sum is 300 rather than an 8-bit wrapped result. Why?
scenarioAnswer: They were promoted before the addition
scenarioWrongs: Char values are not allowed in arithmetic
scenarioWhy: Each unsigned char was promoted to int, and 300 fits in that int.

definition: The operator that yields the remainder after integer division of its left operand by its right operand.
wrongs: The operator that yields the quotient of an integer division.
An operator that computes a floating remainder without a library function.
The operator that performs a bitwise exclusive or.
why: For nonnegative integers, the result is what remains after the largest whole number of divisors is removed.
example: The remainder of 17 divided by 5 is 2.
scenario: A ring buffer uses the remainder when an index is divided by 8. What is the remainder of 11 divided by 8?
scenarioWhy: 11 is one multiple of 8 plus a remainder of 3.

definition: An operator that is true only when both operands are nonzero and that skips the right operand when the left is zero.
wrongs: A bit operator that combines corresponding bits and always evaluates both operands.
An operator that is true when at least one operand is nonzero.
An operator that multiplies its operands.
why: It tests truth values rather than bits, and skipping the right side lets that side depend safely on the left.
example: A test that a pointer is non-null and that the pointee equals 1 does not read the pointee when the pointer is null.
scenario: A condition checks that p is non-null before it reads a member through p. Which operator makes that order safe?
scenarioWhy: Logical AND does not evaluate the member access when the pointer test is false.

definition: An operator that sets each result bit only where both operands have 1, and that evaluates both operands.
wrongs: A truth operator that skips its right operand when the left operand is zero.
An operator that sets a result bit where either operand has a 1.
An operator that inverts every bit of one operand.
why: Each bit position is combined independently, which is how a mask clears or tests selected bits.
example: Combining the bit patterns of 0xF0 and 0x3C with this operator keeps only 0x30.
scenario: A status byte must keep only its low four bits by combining it with the mask 0x0F. Which operator applies the mask?
scenarioWhy: AND with 0x0F clears every bit above the low four and leaves those four bits unchanged.

definition: An operator that moves the bits of an integer toward the high end and fills the vacated low bits with zeros.
wrongs: An operator that moves bits toward the low end and drops the lowest bit.
An operator that rotates bits so a bit leaving one end reenters the other end.
A portable operator that shifts the significand of a float in C source.
why: On an unsigned value, a shift by n that stays within the width multiplies the value by 2 to the n.
example: The unsigned value 1 shifted left by 4 becomes 16.
scenario: An unsigned value 3 is shifted left by 2, and the shift count is within range. What value results?
scenarioWhy: A left shift by 2 multiplies the unsigned value by 4, and 3 times 4 is 12.

definition: The rules that decide which operator is applied first when an expression contains more than one operator.
wrongs: A rule that every expression is grouped strictly left to right, ignoring operator rank.
A rule that parentheses never change grouping in C.
The count of operands an operator accepts.
why: Different operators bind more tightly than others, so an expression has one defined grouping.
example: In a plus b times c, the multiplication is performed before the addition.
scenario: The expression 2 plus 3 times 4 is evaluated with ordinary C precedence. What value does it produce?
scenarioWhy: Multiplication binds more tightly than addition, so the value is 2 plus 12.

definition: The rule that logical AND and logical OR do not evaluate the right operand when the left operand already decides the result.
wrongs: The rule that both operands of a bitwise AND are always evaluated.
The rule that the right operand of the comma operator is skipped.
A guarantee that function arguments are evaluated from right to left.
why: If the left side of AND is false, or the left side of OR is true, the combined result is already known.
example: In a test that n is nonzero and then 10 is divided by n, the division does not run when n is zero.
scenario: The test is that n is not zero and then that 10 divided by n is positive. When n is zero, the division does not run. Which rule prevented it?
scenarioWhy: Logical AND skips the division once the comparison on the left is false.

definition: A statement that runs one branch when its condition is nonzero and an optional else branch otherwise.
wrongs: A loop that repeats its body while a condition stays nonzero.
A multi-way branch that matches an integer against labeled cases.
An unconditional jump to a named label.
why: The condition is tested once, and control enters exactly one of the two branches.
example: If a temperature code is above a limit, firmware turns a fan on; otherwise it turns the fan off.
scenario: One block must run when a flag is nonzero and a different block must run otherwise, with the flag tested once. Which statement fits?
scenarioWhy: A single two-way test is an if statement with an else branch.

definition: A multi-way branch on an integer expression, where execution can continue into the next case if break is omitted.
wrongs: A two-way branch that tests a floating condition.
A loop that repeats every case until a counter ends.
A function that returns the value of the matching case.
why: Case labels do not end a branch by themselves, so control falls into the following case unless something transfers it away.
example: A menu branch for the value 2 also runs the statements of the next case because the first case has no break.
scenario: Case 1 contains no break, the switched value is 1, and the statements under case 2 also run. What caused case 2 to run?
scenarioWhy: Without a break, execution continues from case 1 into the next case.

definition: A loop with an initializer, a condition tested before each body, and an update run after each body.
wrongs: A loop that tests its condition only after the body has already run once.
A multi-way branch on case labels.
A conditional that runs at most one of two blocks.
why: The condition is checked before the body, so the body can run zero times.
example: A loop starts i at 0, continues while i is less than 3, and adds 1 to i, so the body sees 0, 1, and 2.
scenario: A loop must set i to 0, test i before the body, and add 1 to i after the body. Which loop form matches?
scenarioWhy: An initializer, a pretest, and a post-body update are the three parts of a for loop.

definition: A loop that tests its condition before the body and repeats only while that condition is nonzero.
wrongs: A loop that always executes the body once before testing the condition.
A loop that requires a separate update clause between the test and the body.
A branch that chooses one of two blocks and does not repeat.
why: The test occurs first, so a condition that starts false means the body never runs.
example: While a buffer count is positive, a function consumes one byte and then tests the count again.
scenario: A byte count starts at 0, and the body that would consume a byte must not run. Which loop test skips the body?
scenarioWhy: A while loop tests the condition before the body, so a zero count prevents entry.

definition: A statement that leaves the innermost enclosing loop or switch immediately.
wrongs: A statement that skips only the rest of this iteration and continues the loop.
A statement that returns a value from the current function.
A statement that terminates the whole program.
why: Control moves to the statement after the closest loop or switch, rather than to the next iteration.
example: A search loop leaves as soon as the matching index is found, instead of examining the remaining elements.
scenario: A break executes inside the inner of two nested loops. Which loop does it leave?
scenarioWhy: break applies to the innermost enclosing loop or switch.

definition: A statement that skips the rest of the current loop iteration and goes on to the next iteration.
wrongs: A statement that leaves the loop completely.
A statement that exits a switch but has no effect on a loop.
A statement that restarts the program from main.
why: The loop remains active, but statements after continue in the current iteration are not executed.
example: A loop skips the processing of a negative array element and moves on to the next index.
scenario: continue runs in the middle of a for-loop body. What happens next?
scenarioAnswer: The update runs, then the condition is tested
scenarioWrongs: The update is skipped and the body restarts
scenarioWhy: In a for loop, continue jumps to the update expression and then tests the condition again.

definition: A declaration that gives a function's return type and parameter types before a call is compiled.
wrongs: The body of a function, including its local variables.
A macro that textually replaces the function name with a result.
The machine address of the function stored in a pointer at run time.
why: The compiler uses the declared parameter types to check the call and convert the arguments.
example: A header declares a function that takes an int, and a call that passes a double converts that argument.
scenario: A call passes a double to a function declared to take an int, and the argument is converted. What declaration made that conversion known?
scenarioWrongs: The function body in another file with no visible declaration
scenarioWhy: A prototype provides the parameter type used to convert and check the argument.

definition: The rule that a function receives its own copies of argument values rather than aliases of the caller's objects.
wrongs: The rule that a parameter is another name for the caller's object.
The rule that an array argument is copied in full into an array parameter.
The rule that pointer arguments are forbidden.
why: Assigning to a parameter changes only the function's copy, unless the argument is a pointer used to reach the caller's object.
example: A function sets its int parameter to 0, and the caller's int is still 5 after the call returns.
scenario: A function assigns 0 to its int parameter, yet the caller still observes 5. Why did the caller's variable stay unchanged?
scenarioWrongs: The assignment was undefined and discarded
scenarioWhy: C copied the argument into the parameter, so the assignment changed only that copy.

definition: A function calling itself, directly or through another call, until a base case stops the calls.
wrongs: A loop that repeats a body without making another call.
A single call from main to a different function that never calls back.
A macro that is expanded once before compilation.
why: Each invocation has its own parameters and locals, so the function can solve a smaller version of the same problem.
example: A factorial function returns 1 when its argument is 0 and otherwise multiplies the argument by a call on the argument minus 1.
scenario: Computing factorial of 3 calls factorial of 2 before multiplying. What is that self-call?
scenarioWrongs: A loop with no extra call
scenarioWhy: The function invokes itself on a smaller argument, which is recursion.

definition: A contiguous sequence of elements of one type, with the first element at index zero.
wrongs: A chain of elements that are not required to be adjacent in memory.
One object that holds several members of different types at the same time.
A pointer variable that by itself contains every element.
why: Equal-sized elements occupy adjacent slots, so the element at index i lies i slots after the first.
example: Five ints stored in an array occupy indexes 0 through 4 in consecutive memory.
scenario: Five ints lie in adjacent slots and the first valid index is 0. What kind of object holds them?
scenarioWrongs: One pointer that stores all five values
scenarioWhy: Contiguous elements of one type, indexed from zero, form an array.

definition: The conversion, in most expressions, of an array into a pointer to its first element.
wrongs: The copying of every element into a true array parameter.
The conversion of a pointer back into an array that remembers its length.
The deletion of the first element.
why: A parameter declared with array syntax is adjusted to a pointer, so the call passes the address of the first element.
example: A parameter written as an int array of unknown bound actually receives a pointer to the first int.
scenario: A parameter is declared as an int array of unknown bound, and its size equals the size of a pointer. What happened to the caller's array?
scenarioWhy: Array parameters are adjusted to pointers, so the array length is not part of the argument.

definition: An object that stores the address of another object of a stated type, or a null address.
wrongs: An object that stores a copy of an entire array.
An integer that is required to hold the target's value rather than its address.
An alias that must name an object and can never be null.
why: The stored value is an address, and the pointer type says how to interpret the object at that address.
example: A pointer holds the address of an int named x, and reading through the pointer yields x.
scenario: A variable stores the address of an int rather than storing the int itself. What is that variable?
scenarioWhy: An object whose value is the address of another object is a pointer.

definition: The unary operator that produces a pointer to its operand object.
wrongs: The unary operator that reads or writes the object a pointer addresses.
The operator that yields the byte size of a type.
The operator that releases a heap block.
why: Applying it to an object produces a pointer value that refers to that object.
example: Taking the address of an int x produces a value that can be stored in an int pointer.
scenario: A callee must be able to modify the caller's int x, so the call must pass a pointer to x. Which operator creates that pointer?
scenarioWhy: The address of x is a pointer to x, which the callee can use to write x.

definition: The unary operator that designates the object whose address is stored in a pointer.
wrongs: The operator that produces a pointer to an existing object.
The operator that reports how many bytes a type occupies.
The operator that compares two strings.
why: If a pointer holds the address of x, applying this operator reads or writes x.
example: After a pointer addresses x, assigning 4 through that pointer stores 4 in x.
scenario: Pointer p holds the address of x, and the program assigns 4 through the unary operator on p. What happens to x?
scenarioWrongs: p becomes 4 and x is unchanged
x becomes the address of p
scenarioWhy: The operator designates the object p addresses, so the assignment writes x.

definition: Adding an integer n to a pointer to T advances it by n elements of T, not by n bytes unless T is one byte.
wrongs: Adding n always advances every pointer by exactly n bytes.
Adding n advances a pointer by n virtual pages.
C forbids adding an integer to a pointer.
why: The compiler scales the integer by the size of the pointed-to type so the result addresses another element.
example: Adding 1 to an int pointer moves the address forward by the size of one int.
scenario: An int pointer addresses element 0 of an int array, and an int is 4 bytes. What does adding 1 to the pointer address?
scenarioWhy: The addition steps by elements, so plus 1 reaches the next int.

definition: A pointer value that does not address an object and that must not be dereferenced.
wrongs: A pointer that is guaranteed to address a valid int whose value is zero.
The first character of an empty string, which may be read safely.
An uninitialized automatic pointer, which the language sets to null.
why: A null pointer constant compares unequal to every pointer to an object, and using it to access an object is undefined.
example: A failed heap allocation returns a null pointer, and the caller tests it before any access.
scenario: A heap allocation fails and returns a null pointer. What is the defined way to handle that return value?
scenarioAnswer: Test it and do not dereference it
scenarioWrongs: Write through it to force allocation
scenarioWhy: A null return means no object exists, so dereferencing it is undefined.

definition: A generic object pointer that may hold any object's address but cannot be dereferenced until it is converted.
wrongs: A function pointer, which standard C freely converts to and from a void pointer.
A pointer that can be dereferenced to produce a void value.
An integer type used to store character codes.
why: Allocation returns this generic pointer so one function can provide storage for any object type.
example: A void pointer receives the address of an int and is converted to an int pointer before the int is read.
scenario: One parameter must accept the address of either an int or a struct. Which pointer type can hold both object addresses?
scenarioWhy: A void pointer is the generic object pointer and is converted back before it is used.

definition: A sequence of characters stored in an array and ended by a null character.
wrongs: A structure that stores a separate length and may contain a zero byte before the end.
A type that is distinct from an array of char.
An array of ints whose first element stores the length.
why: String functions find the end by scanning for the terminating null character.
example: The letters c, a, and t followed by a zero byte form a string whose length is 3.
scenario: A char array holds the codes for c, a, and t, followed by a zero byte. What does that array contain?
scenarioWhy: A character sequence terminated by a null character is a C string.

definition: The zero character that marks the end of a C string so library functions know where to stop.
wrongs: A leading byte that stores the number of characters in the string.
A pointer with a null value used in place of the character array.
The newline character that ends a line of input.
why: The terminator is a character whose value is zero, and the reported string length does not include it.
example: The length function returns 3 for a three-letter word even though the array also stores a fourth zero byte.
scenario: A length call returns 3 for a char array that occupies 4 bytes and ends in a zero byte. What is that extra byte?
scenarioWhy: The extra zero character ends the string and is excluded from the length.

definition: A library function that compares two strings and returns zero when the strings are equal.
wrongs: A function that returns 1 when the strings are equal and 0 when they differ.
A function that copies the second string over the first.
A function that appends one string to another.
why: The result is negative, zero, or positive according to the lexicographic order of the unsigned character values.
example: Comparing the text cat with cat returns 0, while comparing cat with dog returns a negative value.
scenario: A program calls the standard string compare on two inputs to see whether the text matches. Which return value means they are equal?
scenarioWhy: The compare function returns zero when the characters match through the terminating null.

definition: A type that groups named members, which may have different types, into one object.
wrongs: A type that stores only one of its members at a time, all at the same address.
A sequence whose elements must all have the same type.
A function that returns several values through its name.
why: The members are placed in declaration order, with padding inserted so each member meets its alignment.
example: A point type contains both a float x and a float y in every point object.
scenario: One object must hold an int identifier and a float score at the same time. Which kind of type groups them?
scenarioWhy: A struct can contain members of different types simultaneously.

definition: The operator that selects a struct or union member through a pointer to that struct or union.
wrongs: The dot operator applied directly to a struct object rather than to a pointer.
The operator that dereferences a pointer to a lone int.
The operator that selects an array element by an index.
why: Using it on a pointer is defined as dereferencing that pointer and then selecting the member.
example: If p points at a point structure, the arrow selects the x member of that point.
scenario: Pointer p addresses a struct, and the code must read member id through p. Which operator writes that access directly?
scenarioWrongs: The dot operator applied to p
scenarioWhy: The arrow operator selects a member of the aggregate that a pointer addresses.

definition: A declaration that gives an existing type another name without creating a distinct type.
wrongs: A macro that substitutes text before the compiler checks types.
A definition that always creates a new struct type.
A specifier that gives a variable static storage duration.
why: The alias and the original name are compatible, so they name the same type.
example: An alias named byte for unsigned char still is unsigned char when values of the two names are mixed.
scenario: A header makes byte_t another name for unsigned char, and the two names are the same type. Which feature did that?
scenarioWhy: typedef introduces an alias, so the new name and the original type are identical.

definition: A function that allocates an uninitialized heap block of a requested byte size, or returns null on failure.
wrongs: A function that allocates a block and sets every byte to zero.
A function that releases a block previously obtained from the heap.
A function that changes the size of an existing heap block.
why: The caller chooses the size in bytes and must write the block before reading it, because the bytes are indeterminate.
example: Requesting space for ten ints returns a block large enough for them, and those ints are not yet initialized.
scenario: A program needs 40 uninitialized bytes from the heap and must accept a null result on failure. Which function requests that block?
scenarioWhy: malloc allocates a raw block and does not initialize its contents.

definition: A function that releases a heap block from malloc, calloc, or realloc, and that does nothing if passed null.
wrongs: A function that allocates a new uninitialized block.
A function that also sets the caller's pointer variable to null.
A function that may release the same address twice with defined behavior.
why: The block returns to the heap, but the pointer variable in the caller is left holding its old address.
example: After releasing p, the program assigns null to p so a later mistake is easier to notice.
scenario: A heap block is no longer needed, and passing a null address to the release function must be safe. Which function is that?
scenarioWhy: free deallocates a heap block, and free of a null pointer is defined to do nothing.

definition: A function that allocates an array of objects on the heap and sets every byte of that storage to zero.
wrongs: A function that allocates uninitialized bytes.
A function that releases memory and clears the pointer variable.
A function that reserves an array with automatic storage.
why: The zero fill gives integer objects the value zero before the caller stores anything else.
example: Requesting four ints with this function returns four ints whose values are already 0.
scenario: A program needs four heap ints that are already zero, without assigning zero itself. Which function allocates them?
scenarioWhy: calloc allocates the requested objects and zero-fills their storage.

definition: A function that changes the size of a heap block, possibly moving it, and keeps the old block if it returns null.
wrongs: A function that always grows a block in place and never returns a different address.
A function that releases the old block even when the size change fails.
A function that changes the size of an automatic array.
why: A null return reports failure, and only a non-null return means the caller should start using the possibly new address.
example: Resizing a block to 80 bytes returns a new address, which the program stores back into its pointer.
scenario: A resize of the block addressed by p returns null. What is true of the original block?
scenarioAnswer: It is still allocated and p still addresses it
scenarioWrongs: It was moved and p is invalid
It was cleared and doubled in size
scenarioWhy: A null return means the resize failed and the previous block was not freed.

definition: Heap storage that remains allocated but is no longer reachable, so the program cannot release it.
wrongs: A pointer that still holds the address of storage after that storage was released.
Automatic storage that disappears when its function returns.
A null result from a failed allocation.
why: Without a remaining pointer to the block, there is no address the program can pass to the release function.
example: A function allocates a buffer, then overwrites the only pointer with null and returns without releasing the buffer.
scenario: The only pointer to a heap block is overwritten with null, and the block is never released. What problem was created?
scenarioWhy: The block stays allocated, but the program no longer has an address it can release.

definition: A pointer that still contains the address of storage whose lifetime has already ended.
wrongs: A null pointer, which does not address an object.
The only pointer to a heap block that is still allocated.
A pointer just returned by a successful allocation.
why: The address no longer refers to an object the program owns, so using the pointer is undefined.
example: After a heap block is released, the pointer still holds the old address, and reading through it is invalid.
scenario: A block has been released, the pointer was not cleared, and the code reads through that pointer. What kind of pointer is it?
scenarioWrongs: A pointer that still owns the block
scenarioWhy: The pointer still holds an address of storage that has already been released.

definition: A function that opens a file in a chosen mode and returns a stream pointer, or null if the open fails.
wrongs: A function that flushes and closes an open stream.
A function that writes formatted text to a stream that is already open.
A function that allocates a heap block unrelated to any file.
why: The mode selects reading, writing, or appending, and failure is reported by a null return.
example: Opening a readings file in read mode returns a stream used by later formatted reads.
scenario: A program must open data.txt for reading and receive either a stream or null. Which function does that?
scenarioWhy: fopen creates a stream for a file and returns null when the file cannot be opened.

definition: A function that flushes a stream, closes it, and returns zero when the close succeeds.
wrongs: A function that opens a file and returns a new stream.
A function that releases a heap block.
A function that writes formatted text and leaves the stream open.
why: Closing pushes buffered output to the file and then releases the stream's resources.
example: After several formatted writes, closing the log stream flushes the last buffered text and returns zero.
scenario: Writing to a log is finished, and the buffer must be flushed while the stream is released. Which function does both?
scenarioWrongs: A flush that leaves the stream open
scenarioWhy: fclose flushes buffered data and then closes the stream.

definition: A function that writes formatted output to a chosen stream using a format string and further arguments.
wrongs: A function that writes formatted output only to the standard output stream.
A function that reads formatted input from a stream.
A function that opens a file and returns a stream pointer.
why: The stream argument selects the destination, so the same formatting can target a file rather than the screen.
example: A call passes a log stream and a format string so an error code is written into that file.
scenario: Formatted text must be written to an already open file stream rather than necessarily to the screen. Which function does that?
scenarioWhy: fprintf takes a stream and writes formatted output to it.

definition: The translation phase that handles directives such as include and define before C statements are parsed.
wrongs: The optimizer that removes unused code after types have been checked.
The linker that combines object files into a program.
The loader that places an executable into memory.
why: Directives are processed as tokens early in translation, so they are not ordinary statements that run later.
example: A definition of a buffer size replaces later uses of that name before the compiler type-checks the source.
scenario: A header is inserted and a macro name is replaced before the compiler checks types. Which phase did that work?
scenarioWhy: Include and define are handled before the source is parsed and type-checked.

definition: A define that replaces a name with fixed tokens and does not take arguments.
wrongs: A define whose name is followed by parameters and that substitutes those arguments.
A type alias checked by the compiler as a typedef.
An inline function with a typed parameter list.
why: After the directive, each use of the name is replaced by the given tokens, and there is no parameter list.
example: Defining LIMIT as 10 makes a later expression LIMIT plus 1 become 10 plus 1 before compilation.
scenario: A define gives LIMIT the replacement 10, and LIMIT has no parameter list. What was defined?
scenarioWhy: A define with no parameters is an object-like macro expanded by token replacement.

definition: A macro pattern that causes the body of a header to be processed only once in one translation unit.
wrongs: A runtime lock that stops two tasks from reading one header.
A compiler switch that disables every include.
A linker option that pulls in a library only once.
why: The first inclusion defines the guard macro, and a later inclusion skips the body because that macro is already defined.
example: A header tests whether its guard macro is defined, defines it, and skips the struct on a second inclusion.
scenario: A header included twice does not redefine its struct, because a macro was defined on the first inclusion. What pattern skipped the second body?
scenarioWhy: The guard macro makes the second inclusion skip the contents of the header.

definition: A program construct for which the C standard places no requirements on the implementation.
wrongs: Behaviour the standard fully specifies, such as unsigned wraparound.
A diagnostic that every compiler is required to print at compile time.
Behaviour an implementation must choose and document.
why: After such a construct occurs, later execution has no portable meaning that a program may rely on.
example: Adding 1 to the maximum signed int is undefined behaviour.
scenario: A program adds 1 to the maximum value of a signed int. How does the C standard classify that overflow?
scenarioWhy: Signed overflow is undefined, whereas unsigned overflow is defined to wrap.

definition: A local variable with static storage duration that is initialized only once and keeps its value between calls.
wrongs: An automatic local that is created again on every entry to the function.
A file-scope variable that other translation units can name with extern.
A variable the compiler is required to place in a hardware register.
why: The object lives for the whole program, while its name is visible only inside the block where it is declared.
example: A function's static counter starts at 0 and rises by 1 on each call instead of restarting.
scenario: A function has a static int count initialized to 0, and each call adds 1. What value does the third call see before adding 1?
scenarioWhy: The variable is initialized once, so the third entry sees the two increments performed by the earlier calls.
